s.d: pertaining to being wet or moist
s.g: wet; moist; green (in reference to wood)

s.d: a container for storing or carrying water or other liquids; made of stone or clay
s.g: pitcher; water jar

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.g: to drink water
s.c: In a number of languages ‘to drink water’ is expressed by a single term which combines the components of drinking and of water. In other instances a verb meaning simply ‘to drink’ normally means to drink water unless otherwise specified. In Greek almost the opposite situation exists. For example, ⟦Matthew 11:18|Matthew 11:18⟧ (ἦλθεν γὰρ Ἰωάννης μήτε ἐσθίων μήτε πίνων ‘for John came neither eating nor drinking’) implies a reference to drinking alcoholic beverages.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: pertaining to swelling resulting from the accumulation of lymph in the body tissues
s.g: suffering from dropsy

s.d: a clear liquid that is without color, taste, or smell in its pure form; it forms rivers, lakes, and oceans, and sustains life on earth
s.g: water
s.c: In ⟦2 Peter 3:5|2 Peter 3:5⟧ the Greek expression is admittedly both strange and obscure. ἐξ ὕδατος presumably refers to the fact that the land emerged from the water, or at least was separated from the water. The phrase δἰ ὕδατος, literally ‘through water,’ may be locative, that is to say, it may refer to a place, but it is more likely to have some reference to water as an instrument which contributed to the act of producing the heavens and earth. However, the active instrument for this creation was τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγῳ ‘the word of God.’. Since the dative case ὕδατι ‘by water’ is clearly instrumental in verse 6, it may be that ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ δἰ ὕδατος in verse 5 refers in a spacial sense to the formation of the heavens and the dry land ‘from water and through a watery area.’|Even more complex, however, than the interpretation of ‘water’ in ⟦2 Peter 3:5|2 Peter 3:5⟧ is the fact that in a number of languages there are quite different terms for ὕδωρ depending upon the type of water, its location, and its function. For example, water in some kind of bowl or container (and thus most likely used for drinking or cooking) may be referred to by one term, while water in a lake, stream, or ocean may be identified by quite a different term. Similarly, an important distinction may be made between salt water and fresh water, and an even further distinction may be introduced in the case of brackish water, that is to say, water which is partially salty. Some languages make a distinction between water which collects in pools and water which is flowing in streams or rivers. Accordingly, careful attention must be paid to contexts in order to select the appropriate term for ὕδωρ (see also LN 8.64 on ⟦John 19:34|John 19:34⟧).

s.d: water that falls in drops condensed from water vapor in the atmosphere
s.g: rain; rain water
s.c: Though ὑετός, which means rain as a substance (for ‘the event of raining,’ see LN 14.10), generally occurs in contexts in which the focus is upon the ‘the event of raining,’ as supplied by a verb (for example, ⟦Acts 14:17|Acts 14:17⟧; ⟦James 5:18|James 5:18⟧; and ⟦Revelation 11:6|Revelation 11:6⟧), in ⟦Hebrews 6:7|Hebrews 6:7⟧ the focus is clearly upon the substance. Though the Greek text of ⟦Hebrews 6:7|Hebrews 6:7⟧ speaks literally of the ground ‘drinking the rain,’ this figurative expression can rarely be reproduced. Sometimes one can use an expression such as ‘soaks up,’ the type of term which might be employed in speaking of a sponge soaking up moisture, but in a number of instances one can only speak of ‘the rain disappearing into the earth’ or ‘the earth causing the rain to disappear into it.’|Translators may be confronted with several problems in selecting an appropriate term for ‘rain,’ since some languages make important distinctions in terms for ‘rain’ depending upon the season of the year and the quantity of rain. For example, rain falling in the dry season may be called by quite a different term from that which falls in the rainy season. Similarly, a series of distinctions may be made in terms for rain depending upon whether one is speaking of a torrential rainstorm or an average rain or a continuous mist.

s.d: rain, whether light or torrential
s.g: rain; to rain
s.c: Though most languages have a general term for rain, the event of raining is more frequently referred to by a verb rather than by a noun, since rain is something which takes place and is not regarded as a thing or mass, unless, of course, one is referring to the water which comes down as rain, that is to say, ‘rain water’ (see LN 2.10). In some languages the event of raining is generally expressed idiomatically as ‘God is urinating.’ This might appear unduly crude and anthropomorphic, but to the speakers of such a language the expression is often quite acceptable and has no undesirable connotations.|Though in English one may use an impersonal subject with the verb ‘to rain,’ for example, ‘it is raining,’ many languages require some kind of personal agent, for example, ‘God is raining,’ or an impersonal agent such as ‘the sky is raining’ or ‘the clouds are raining.’

s.d: to formally and legally declare that someone who is not one’s own child is henceforth to be treated and cared for as one’s own child, including complete rights of inheritance
s.g: to adopt; adoption
s.c: In a number of languages adoption is spoken of as ‘making a child a son’ or ‘causing a child to become a daughter.’ In some instances the equivalent expression is merely ‘to treat someone as a son’ or ‘… daughter.’

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: an immediate male offspring
s.g: son

s.dp: People › Persons For Whom There Is Affectionate Concern
s.d: (extension of meaning of {L:υἱός<SDBG:υἱός:000000>}[a] ‘son,’ {D:10.42}) a person of any age for whom there is a special relationship of endearment and association
s.g: my child; my dear friend; my dear man; my dear one; my dear lad
s.c: The usage of υἱός in ⟦Hebrews 12:5|Hebrews 12:5⟧ reflects the relationship between a spiritual father or teacher and a follower.

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: (an extended meaning of {L:υἱός<SDBG:υἱός:000000>}[a] ‘son,’ {D:10.42}) a non-immediate male descendant (possibly involving a gap of several generations){N:001}
s.g: male descendant
s.c: Though υἱός is often translated as ‘son,’ speaking, for example, of ‘Joseph son of David,’ this may be very misleading in some languages, since readers would assume that a ‘son’ belonged to an immediately following generation. In some instances a term such as ‘great grandson’ is generalized to mean any individual in the third or in any one of a number of succeeding generations. In place of a phrase such as ‘descendant of David,’ it is sometimes necessary to invert the expression to read ‘David was one of his ancestors.’

s.d: the male offspring of an animal (occurring in the NT only with {L:ὑποζύγιον<SDBG:ὑποζύγιον:000000>} ‘beast of burden,’ {D:4.7})
s.g: foal; offspring
s.c: See the discussion of ⟦Matthew 21:5|Matthew 21:5⟧ in LN 4.7.

s.d: (followed by the genitive of class or kind) a person of a class or kind, specified by the following genitive construction
s.g: son of …; person of …; one who is …
s.c: For a discussion of υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, see LN 12.15.|In most languages it is difficult, if not impossible, to represent adequately the meaning of such expressions consisting of the formula ‘son of …’ without making some significant adjustments. For example, ‘your sons’ in ⟦Matthew 12:27|Matthew 12:27⟧ may be rendered as ‘your followers.’ In ⟦Acts 13:10|Acts 13:10⟧ ‘son of the Devil’ may be rendered as ‘you are like the Devil,’ while in ⟦Luke 16:8|Luke 16:8⟧ ‘sons of this age’ may be readily translated as ‘people who are typical of this age.’ In ⟦Matthew 23:15|Matthew 23:15⟧ ‘son of Gehenna’ may be rendered as ‘you who deserve to go to hell,’ and in ⟦Mark 3:17|Mark 3:17⟧ ‘sons of thunder’ may be rendered as ‘men who are like thunder’ or ‘thunderous persons.’ For idiomatic expressions involving ‘sons of …,’ see LN 11.13, LN 11.14, and LN 11.16.

s.dp: Guide, Discipline, Follow › Follow, Be a Disciple
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:υἱός<SDBG:υἱός:000000>}[a] ‘son,’ {D:10.42}) one who is a disciple or follower of someone, with the implication of being like the one whom he follows (a reflection of the Semitic use of υἱός in the expression son of)
s.g: disciple; follower
s.c: In ⟦1 Peter 5:13|1 Peter 5:13⟧ the meaning of the expression Μᾶρκος ὁ υἱός μου, literally ‘Mark, my son,’ may be ‘Mark, my disciple’ or ‘Mark, my follower.’ On the other hand, υἱός may simply be a means of referring to a younger person in an affectionate manner (see LN 9.46).

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: a member of a sociopolitical group with some presumed ethnic relationship
s.g: citizen

s.d: a kind or class of persons, with the implication of possessing certain derived characteristics
s.g: son of; offspring of; child of; kind of; one who has the characteristics of; person of

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: (an idiom, literally: sons of Israel) the people of Israel as an ethnic entity
s.g: the people of Israel; the nation of Israel
s.c: In translating the expression ‘the people of Israel’ it may be necessary to use an appositional phrase, for example, ‘the people, namely, Israel’ or a relative clause which also serves an appositional function, for example, ‘the people who are Israel.’ In some languages it may be preferable to use a term such as ‘nation’ followed by some expression which will indicate that Israel is simply the name of the nation, for example, ‘the nation called Israel.’

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: (an idiom, literally: sons of the kingdom) people who should properly be or were traditionally regarded as a part of the kingdom of God
s.g: people of God’s kingdom; God’s people
s.c: In a number of languages a literal rendering of ‘sons of the kingdom’ would be relatively meaningless. It is normally possible to use a descriptive phrase in contexts such as ⟦Matthew 8:12|Matthew 8:12⟧, for example, ‘those who should be a part of the kingdom of God’ or ‘those over whom God should be ruling.’ In this context, as well as in most others, the Greek term traditionally rendered ‘kingdom’ (in speaking of ‘the kingdom of God’) points essentially to the rule of God rather than to any place or time. See also LN 37.64.

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: (an idiom, literally: sons of this age) persons who hold to the value system of the world
s.g: non-religious people; people of this world; people of this age
s.c: In some instances ‘the people of this world’ may be rendered as ‘the people who live like most people in the world’ or ‘the people who are concerned only about what people say.’ Sometimes the identification with the world is expressed in contrast with people’s attitude concerning God, for example, ‘people who have no use for God.’

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › General
s.d: (an idiom, literally: sons of the wedding hall) guests at a wedding, or more specifically, friends of the bridegroom participating in wedding festivities
s.g: wedding guests or friends of the bridegroom
s.c: A literal rendering of the idiom ‘sons of the wedding hall’ has often been seriously misunderstood, for example, the bride’s children born prior to the marriage.

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: (idioms, literally: sons of the light, and: sons of the day) persons to whom the truth of God has been revealed and who are presumably living according to such truth. See also {D:9.4} and {D:12.15}
s.g: sons of the light; children of the light; people of God
s.c: In a number of languages it is difficult to speak of ‘light’ in the metaphorical sense of the truth that comes from God. Such truth is not to be equated with knowledge, but with the principles and practices of right moral behavior. Because of these difficulties in speaking of ‘truth’ as ‘light,’ a number of translators have preferred to use the expression ‘people of God’ for the phrases υἱοὶ τοῦ φωτός, υἱοὶ τῆς ἡμέρας, and τέκνα φωτός. In some instances, however, it is possible to employ ‘light,’ if this is described as ‘light that comes from God’ or even ‘the true light from God.’|Though there are two expressions, υἱοὶ φωτός and υἱοὶ ἡμέρας, in ⟦1 Thessalonians 5:5|1 Thessalonians 5:5⟧, there does not seem to be any significant difference in meaning. The two phrases simply supplement and reinforce each other.

s.d: (a Semitic idiom, literally: sons of men) human beings (equivalent in denotative meaning to {L:ἄνθρωπος<SDBG:ἄνθρωπος:000000>}[a], {D:9.1})
s.g: people; mankind
s.c: It is rare indeed that one can reproduce literally the Semitic phrase ‘sons of men,’ since the expression is likely to be interpreted as relating only to the male offspring of fathers.

s.d: a title with Messianic implications used by Jesus concerning himself
s.g: Son of Man
s.c: This title ‘Son of Man’ served not only to affirm but also to hide Christ’s Messianic role.|In a number of languages there are serious complications involved in a literal translation of υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ‘Son of Man.’ In the first place, this is likely to be understood in a more or less literal sense of ‘son of a man’ and thus a denial of the virgin birth. Such is particularly true in languages which have two words for ‘son,’ one meaning ‘son of a man’ and the other, ‘son of a woman.’ Under such circumstances, a literal translation would be a clear denial of the virgin birth.

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: (a title applied to Jesus, literally: son of God; parallel in semantic structure to phrases consisting of υἱός followed by the genitive of class or kind; compare {D:9.4}) one who has the essential characteristics and nature of God
s.g: Son of God
s.c: Before adopting a translation of υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ such as ‘Son of God,’ one must always investigate the extent to which such an expression might already be used in a particular language. For example, in the Tarahumara language of Mexico mankind is divided into two classes: (1) ‘sons of God,’ who are Tarahumaras and (2) ‘sons of the devil,’ all other people. In these circumstances it is necessary in translating υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ to use an expression which will identify ‘the unique Son of God’ or ‘the one who is truly the Son of God.’

s.d: a title applied to Jesus, with Messianic implications, emphasizing Jesus’ link to David
s.g: son of David

s.d: a dense growth of trees covering a relatively large area
s.g: forest
s.c: In ⟦James 3:5|James 3:5⟧ it is also possible to interpret ὕλη as wood which has been cut up, either firewood or wood used for construction (see ὕλη wood, pile of wood, LN 3.64).|In some languages spoken by people living in tropical forest areas the equivalent of ‘forest’ is simply the expression ‘where no one lives,’ based upon the fact that people live in clearings and everything else is forest. Such a rendering, however, may not lead to a satisfactory translation of ⟦James 3:5|James 3:5⟧ (the only occurrence of ὕλη in the NT), in which case one is better advised to interpret ὕλη in the sense of ‘pile of wood’ (LN 3.64).

s.d: the woody part of trees or bushes
s.g: wood; pile of wood
s.c: In ⟦James 3:5|James 3:5⟧ ὕλη may be interpreted as a forest (see LN 3.3).|As already noted in the case of ξύλον (LN 3.60), a number of languages make a distinction between wood used as building material and wood employed in heating or cooking.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person who defected from true faith
s.g: Hymenaeus

s.d: pertaining to receptors
s.g: your; yours; of you

s.d: to sing a song associated with religion and worship
s.g: to sing a hymn; to sing a song of praise

s.d: a song with religious content
s.g: hymn

s.d: to continue to move along
s.g: to move along; to go along

s.dp: Linear Movement › Leave, Depart, Flee, Escape, Send
s.d: to move away from a reference point, perhaps more definitively than in the case of {L:πορεύομαι<SDBG:πορεύομαι:000002>}[c] and {L:ἄγω<SDBG:ἄγω:000002>}[c] ({D:15.34})
s.g: to go; to go away from; to depart; to leave

s.dp: Linear Movement › Leave, Depart, Flee, Escape, Send
s.d: to depart from someone’s presence, with the implication of a changed relation
s.g: to depart; to leave; to go away

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: to depart from life, as a euphemistic expression for death{N:002}
s.g: to leave this life; to die; death; departure

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Change of State
s.d: to undergo a significant change
s.g: to undergo; to go to
s.c: It is also possible to interpret ὑπάγω in ⟦Revelation 17:8|Revelation 17:8⟧ as ‘to experience a state’ (Domain 90M), and there may be in the context of ⟦Revelation 17:8|Revelation 17:8⟧ some aspect of movement (Domain 15).

s.d: to obey on the basis of having paid attention to{N:001}
s.g: to obey; obedience
s.c: Terms expressing the concept of ‘obedience’ may frequently be rendered in some languages as ‘to do what one says’ or ‘to carry out someone’s orders.’

s.d: to obey on the basis of having paid attention to{N:001}
s.g: to obey; obedience
s.c: Terms expressing the concept of ‘obedience’ may frequently be rendered in some languages as ‘to do what one says’ or ‘to carry out someone’s orders.’

s.d: to respond to someone knocking or calling at a door
s.g: to answer the door

s.d: pertaining to being legally bound to a man in marriage
s.g: married

s.d: to come near to and to meet, either in a friendly or hostile sense
s.g: to draw near; to meet; to meet up with
s.c: In a number of languages it is necessary to specify clearly by the choice of terms whether the meeting is friendly or hostile.

s.d: to oppose in battle
s.g: to meet in battle; to face in battle

s.d: to come near to and to meet, either in a friendly or hostile sense
s.g: to draw near; to meet; to meet up with
s.c: In a number of languages it is necessary to specify clearly by the choice of terms whether the meeting is friendly or hostile.

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Have, Possess, Property, Owner
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὑπάρχω<SDBG:ὑπάρχω:000003>}[d] ‘to belong to,’ {D:57.2}) that which constitutes someone’s possession{N:001}
s.g: possessions; property

s.d: to be in a state, normally with the implication of a particular set of circumstances
s.g: to be

s.d: to be identical with{N:001}
s.g: to be

s.d: to exist, particularly in relation to ownership
s.g: to exist; to belong to

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Have, Possess, Property, Owner
s.d: to belong to someone{N:002}
s.g: to belong to; to have

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Have, Possess, Property, Owner
s.d: (neuter plural participle of {L:ὑπάρχω<SDBG:ὑπάρχω:000003>}[d] ‘to belong to,’ {D:57.2}) that which constitutes someone’s possession{N:003}
s.g: possessions; property

s.d: to submit to the orders or directives of someone
s.g: to obey; to submit to; obedience; submission

s.d: pertaining to being hostile toward{N:001}
s.g: hostile; one who is hostile

s.d: (with the genitive) a marker of a participant who is benefited by an event or on whose behalf an event takes place
s.g: for; on behalf of; for the sake of
s.c: In a number of languages, one cannot speak of ‘doing something on behalf of sins’; only a person can be benefited by an event, and therefore one must translate ‘who gave himself on behalf of us who had sinned’ in ⟦Galatians 1:4|Galatians 1:4⟧. See also LN 90.39.

s.d: (with the genitive) a marker of general content, whether of a discourse or mental activity{N:001}
s.g: concerning; about; of

s.dp: Degree › More Than, Less Than [Comparative Degree]
s.d: a degree which is beyond that of a compared scale of extent
s.g: more than; to a greater degree than; beyond

s.dp: Status › High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
s.d: a marker of status which is superior to another status
s.g: above; superior to

s.d: a marker of cause or reason, often with the implication of something which has been beneficial
s.g: because of; in view of

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Arrogance, Haughtiness, Pride
s.d: to become puffed up with pride, with the probable implication of being disparaging toward others
s.g: to be overly proud; to be puffed up with pride; to feel overly self-confident

s.d: to exalt oneself in pride against someone or something
s.g: to rise up in pride against
s.c: ὑπεραίρω involves two distinct types of components: (1) the development of opposition, and (2) the psychological basis for such opposition, namely, pride. In almost all instances it will be necessary to represent the two complementary components by a phrasal equivalent, for example, ‘to be proud and to rise up against’ or ‘because of one’s pride, to rise up in opposition to.’

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: pertaining to being of an age beyond the prime of life (in {S:04600703600024} a reference to a woman beyond the normal marriageable age){N:001}
s.g: past one’s prime; past marriageable age

s.d: a position above another, whether or not in contact
s.g: above; over; on; upon

s.dp: Status › High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
s.d: a marker of superior status, suggesting an additional factor of degree
s.g: far above; considerably superior to

s.d: to increase exceedingly in the degree of a state
s.g: to increase greatly

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sin, Wrongdoing, Guilt
s.d: to transgress the will and law of God by going beyond prescribed limits
s.g: to transgress; to sin against

s.dp: Degree › More Than, Less Than [Comparative Degree]
s.d: an extraordinary degree, involving a considerable excess over what would be expected (this series differs from the series in {D:78.31} primarily in emphasizing the excessive degree)
s.g: extreme; extremely; to an extreme degree; to a very great degree

s.dp: Degree › More Than, Less Than [Comparative Degree]
s.d: a degree which exceeds extraordinarily a point on an implied or overt scale of extent{N:001}
s.g: extraordinary; extreme; supreme; far more; much greater; to a far greater degree
s.c: There are obviously a number of problems involved in attempting to render an expression of extraordinary degree, but it is sometimes possible to express such a degree by building up a series of intensive markers. For example, in ⟦Ephesians 2:7|Ephesians 2:7⟧ one might translate τὸ ὑπερβάλλον πλοῦτος τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ as ‘his very, very great grace,’ and in ⟦2 Corinthians 4:7|2 Corinthians 4:7⟧ one might render ἡ ὑπερβολὴ τῆς δυνάμεως ᾖ τοῦ θεοῦ as ‘God has very, very great power.’ Such expressions, however, may not do full justice to the intensity of degree expressed in ὑπερβάλλω and ὑπερβολή, since in a number of languages the closest equivalent might be something involving figurative meanings. For example, τὸ ὑπερβάλλον πλοῦτος τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ in ⟦Ephesians 2:7|Ephesians 2:7⟧ might be rendered as ‘he is gracious beyond anything we can imagine,’ and in ⟦2 Corinthians 4:7|2 Corinthians 4:7⟧ ἡ ὑπερβολὴ τῆς δυνάμεως ᾖ τοῦ θεοῦ may be rendered as ‘God has power beyond any words to describe.’|In this expression in ⟦Ephesians 2:7|Ephesians 2:7⟧, both ὑπερβάλλον and πλοῦτος (LN 78.15) serve as expressions of degree; ὑπερβάλλον indicates an implied comparison, while πλοῦτος suggests not only a high degree of something, but also value.

s.dp: Degree › More Than, Less Than [Comparative Degree]
s.d: a degree which exceeds extraordinarily a point on an implied or overt scale of extent{N:001}
s.g: extraordinary; extreme; supreme; far more; much greater; to a far greater degree
s.c: There are obviously a number of problems involved in attempting to render an expression of extraordinary degree, but it is sometimes possible to express such a degree by building up a series of intensive markers. For example, in ⟦Ephesians 2:7|Ephesians 2:7⟧ one might translate τὸ ὑπερβάλλον πλοῦτος τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ as ‘his very, very great grace,’ and in ⟦2 Corinthians 4:7|2 Corinthians 4:7⟧ one might render ἡ ὑπερβολὴ τῆς δυνάμεως ᾖ τοῦ θεοῦ as ‘God has very, very great power.’ Such expressions, however, may not do full justice to the intensity of degree expressed in ὑπερβάλλω and ὑπερβολή, since in a number of languages the closest equivalent might be something involving figurative meanings. For example, τὸ ὑπερβάλλον πλοῦτος τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ in ⟦Ephesians 2:7|Ephesians 2:7⟧ might be rendered as ‘he is gracious beyond anything we can imagine,’ and in ⟦2 Corinthians 4:7|2 Corinthians 4:7⟧ ἡ ὑπερβολὴ τῆς δυνάμεως ᾖ τοῦ θεοῦ may be rendered as ‘God has power beyond any words to describe.’

s.dp: Spacial Positions › Beyond, On the Other Side Of
s.d: a position farther away than a reference point
s.g: beyond; farther away

s.d: to engage in an activity beyond some implied limit, whether in intensity or extent
s.g: to overextend; to stretch out beyond; to overstep a limit
s.c: There are significant differences of opinion with regard to the interpretation of ⟦2 Corinthians 10:14|2 Corinthians 10:14⟧, and these differences should no doubt be reflected in marginal notes.

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
s.d: to pour or run out over, either of a liquid or a dry mass
s.g: to overflow; to flow over; to run over

s.d: to intercede on behalf of someone, with specific emphasis upon the fact that what is being done is for the sake of someone else{N:001}
s.g: to intercede on behalf of; to intercede for

s.d: to be of surpassing or exceptional value
s.g: to be exceptionally valuable; to surpass in value; to be better

s.d: to exercise continuous control over someone or something
s.g: to control; to restrain
s.c: There is usually no difficulty in speaking of ‘control’ if it is performed by a person as in ⟦1 Peter 2:13|1 Peter 2:13⟧. However, it may not be possible to speak of ‘death’ having control, unless the language in question can personify death. In some instances ⟦Acts 2:24|Acts 2:24⟧ (see LN 37.16) must be rendered as ‘it was impossible for him to continue to be dead,’ and in ⟦2 Corinthians 5:14|2 Corinthians 5:14⟧ ‘Christ’s love controls us’ may be rendered as ‘the fact that Christ loves us causes us to act as we do.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Arrogance, Haughtiness, Pride
s.d: a state of ostentatious pride or arrogance bordering on insolence
s.g: pride; arrogance; haughtiness

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Arrogance, Haughtiness, Pride
s.d: pertaining to being ostentatiously proud
s.g: arrogant; haughty; contemptuous

s.dp: Degree › More Than, Less Than [Comparative Degree]
s.d: an extraordinary degree, involving a considerable excess over what would be expected (this series differs from the series in {D:78.31} primarily in emphasizing the excessive degree)
s.g: extreme; extremely; to an extreme degree; to a very great degree
s.c: In order that something of the irony of the phrase τῶν ὑπερλίαν ἀποστόλων (⟦2 Corinthians 11:5|2 Corinthians 11:5⟧) may be indicated, one may wish to follow the example of Today’s English Version and translate “I do not think that I am the least bit inferior to those very special so-called ‘apostles’ of yours!”

s.d: to be completely and overwhelmingly victorious
s.g: to be completely victorious; to have complete victory over

s.d: pertaining to excessive boasting
s.g: boastful
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ‘boastful words’ is ‘words too big for what one is talking about’ or ‘puffed up words’ or ‘swollen words.’

s.dp: Think › To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
s.d: to intentionally not regard or be concerned about certain objects or events
s.g: to overlook; to purposely pay no attention to; disregard

s.dp: Status › High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
s.d: a state of high rank or position, with the implication in some contexts of being too high or excessive
s.g: high status; high sounding; pompous

s.d: to be more abundant than a given quantity
s.g: to be more than; to be more abundant
s.c: For another interpretation of ὑπερπερισσεύω in ⟦Romans 5:20|Romans 5:20⟧, see LN 78.34.

s.dp: Degree › More Than, Less Than [Comparative Degree]
s.d: an extraordinary degree, involving a considerable excess over what would be expected (this series differs from the series in {D:78.31} primarily in emphasizing the excessive degree)
s.g: extreme; extremely; to an extreme degree; to a very great degree
s.c: Though it is possible to interpret ὑπερπερισσεύω in ⟦Romans 5:20|Romans 5:20⟧ as referring simply to quantity (see LN 59.49), it is better to interpret it as expressing degree. χάρις itself indicates the activity of God in showing favor, and ὑπερπερισσεύω is simply an expression of abundant degree involved in such an activity.

s.dp: Degree › More Than, Less Than [Comparative Degree]
s.d: an extraordinary degree, involving a considerable excess over what would be expected (this series differs from the series in {D:78.31} primarily in emphasizing the excessive degree)
s.g: extreme; extremely; to an extreme degree; to a very great degree

s.d: to be more abundant than a given quantity
s.g: to be more than; to be more abundant
s.c: In a number of languages it may be difficult to indicate the overabundance of grace in ⟦1 Timothy 1:14|1 Timothy 1:14⟧, since there is nothing in the context to provide a basis for comparison. Accordingly, the closest equivalent may be ‘but the grace of our Lord was very, very much.’

s.dp: Status › Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
s.d: to regard a person as being exceptionally honored in view of high status
s.g: to give exceptional honor

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Arrogance, Haughtiness, Pride
s.d: to have an unwarranted pride in oneself or in one’s accomplishments
s.g: to be conceited; to be arrogant; to be proud; to think highly of oneself

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: a room on the level above the ground floor (second story in American usage and first story in most other languages)
s.g: upstairs room
s.c: In ⟦Acts 1:13|Acts 1:13⟧, ⟦Acts 9:37|Acts 9:37⟧, ⟦Acts 9:39|Acts 9:39⟧, ⟦Acts 20:8|Acts 20:8⟧ the term ὑπερῷον may refer to the kind of rooms often built on the flat-roofed Middle East housetops.

s.d: to experience something to which a person is subjected
s.g: to be subjected to; to experience; to undergo; to suffer

s.d: (derivative of {L:ὑπακούω<SDBG:ὑπακούω:000000>}[a] ‘to obey,’ {D:36.15}) pertaining to being obedient
s.g: obedient

s.d: to render assistance or help by performing certain duties, often of a humble or menial nature
s.g: to serve; to render service; to help; service; help
s.c: In some languages it is essential in communicating the concept of ‘service’ to introduce a specific reference to ‘a servant,’ for example, ‘to help as a servant’ or ‘to assist as one who must,’ and in some contexts it may be useful to employ a phrase such as ‘to help in small things’ or ‘to do the low tasks.’

s.dp: Help, Care For › Provide For, Support
s.d: to provide continuous and possibly prolonged assistance and help by supplying the needs of someone
s.g: to provide for; to support

s.d: (derivative of {L:ὑπηρετέω<SDBG:ὑπηρετέω:000000>}[a] ‘to serve,’ {D:35.19}) a person who renders service
s.g: servant
s.c: In rendering θεράπων, ὑπηρέτης, and διάκονος in the sense of ‘servant,’ it is important to avoid a term which would be too specific, for example, ‘one who serves meals’ or ‘one who works around the house.’ It may, in fact, be necessary to use an expression which means essentially ‘helper.’|In the NT ὑπηρέτης is employed to refer to many diverse types of servants, such as attendants to a king, officers of the Sanhedrin, attendants of magistrates, and, especially in the Gospel of John, Jewish Temple guards.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sleep, Waking
s.d: the state of being asleep
s.g: to sleep; to be asleep; sleep
s.c: In some languages sleep is expressed by an idiom, for example, ‘his soul had wandered away’ or ‘his eyes had disappeared.’ Though an expression such as ‘his soul had wandered away’ might appear in some languages to have misleading theological implications, it really means only ‘to sleep.’

s.d: a position below another position or object
s.g: under

s.d: (with the accusative) a marker of a controlling person, institution, or power
s.g: under; under the control of; under obligation to
s.c: It is generally a mistake to render literally the expression τοὺς ὑπὸ νόμον as in ⟦Galatians 4:5|Galatians 4:5⟧, because ‘those who are under the Law’ may simply mean ‘people who act illegally.’

s.dp: Case › Agent, Personal or Nonpersonal, Causative or Immediate, Direct or Indirect
s.d: (with the genitive) a marker of agent or force, whether person or event
s.g: by
s.c: In a number of languages it is difficult, if not impossible, to use a so-called passive expression which introduces an agent by means of a preposition. It may, therefore, be necessary in a number of instances to make the agent the subject of the sentence or clause. For example, ⟦Mark 1:13|Mark 1:13⟧ may be restructured as ‘Satan tempted Jesus when Jesus was in the desert for forty days.’

s.d: a marker of cause or reason, with focus upon instrumentality, either of objects or events
s.g: because of; on account of; by reason of

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: a marker of the approximate time of a period (a rare usage)
s.g: about; at

s.dp: Courts and Legal Procedures › Judge, Condemn, Acquit
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to fall under judgment) to be condemned for acting contrary to laws and regulations
s.g: to be condemned; to suffer condemnation; to be judged guilty
s.c: In the context of ⟦James 5:12|James 5:12⟧ the condemnation refers to God’s judgment.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › The Earth's Surface
s.d: (an idiom, literally: under the sky) pertaining to being on the earth
s.g: on earth
s.c: ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανόν is essentially equivalent in reference to ἐπίγειος ‘on the earth’ (LN 1.41).

s.d: to be under the complete control of someone
s.g: under the complete control of
s.c: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to preserve the idiom ‘under the feet of,’ though in some instances one may use a parallel idiom, for example, ‘to stand on,’ so that ⟦1 Corinthians 15:25|1 Corinthians 15:25⟧ might be rendered ‘until he stands on all his enemies,’ but it is more likely that the idiom in this context is better rendered as ‘until he defeats all his enemies.’

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Hire, Rent Out
s.d: to hire a person to act in a particular way, often involving dishonest activities
s.g: to hire; to bribe; to induce

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Pattern, Model, Example, and Corresponding Representation
s.d: a model of behavior as an example to be imitated or to be avoided
s.g: model; example

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Pattern, Model, Example, and Corresponding Representation
s.d: a model of behavior as an example to be imitated or to be avoided
s.g: model; example

s.dp: Know › Well Known, Clearly Shown, Revealed
s.d: to make known the character or significance of something by visual, auditory, gestural, or linguistic means{N:001}
s.g: to make known; to demonstrate; to show
s.c: In some languages it may be useful to translate ὑποδείκνυμι in ⟦Acts 20:35|Acts 20:35⟧ as ‘I showed you by example’ or ‘I demonstrated by example’ or ‘I showed you by what I did.’

s.d: to explain the meaning or significance of something by demonstration{N:002}
s.g: to show; to explain; to make clear

s.d: to accept the presence of a person with friendliness{N:001}
s.g: to welcome; to receive; to accept; to have as a guest

s.d: to put on and wear footwear (shoes, boots, or sandals)
s.g: to put on; to tie on; to wear (footwear)

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: any type of footwear  (though ordinarily the reference would be to a sandal rather than to a shoe)
s.g: sandal; shoe

s.dp: Courts and Legal Procedures › Judicial Hearing, Inquiry
s.d: pertaining to being subject to justifying behavior before a court of justice
s.g: answerable to; liable to judgment

s.d: an animal which can be used to carry a burden or can be ridden
s.g: pack animal; beast of burden; riding animal
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 21:5|Matthew 21:5⟧ it may not actually be necessary to translate ‘the offspring of a beast of burden’ (υἱὸν ὑποζυγίου), since this may be regarded as being completely redundant after speaking of a donkey and her colt. In some languages it may be necessary in certain contexts to indicate the sex of a donkey. In ⟦2 Peter 2:16|2 Peter 2:16⟧ the reference of ὑποζύγιον is a female donkey, as indicated in the Hebrew text of ⟦Numbers 22:22|Numbers 22:22⟧.

s.d: (a technical, nautical term) to brace a ship
s.g: to fasten ropes around; to brace

s.d: a position below another position or object
s.g: under

s.d: a position on the undersurface of an object
s.g: under; on

s.d: to be under the complete control of someone
s.g: under the complete control of
s.c: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to preserve the idiom ‘under the feet of,’ though in some instances one may use a parallel idiom, for example, ‘to stand on,’ so that ⟦1 Corinthians 15:25|1 Corinthians 15:25⟧ might be rendered ‘until he stands on all his enemies,’ but it is more likely that the idiom in this context is better rendered as ‘until he defeats all his enemies.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Hypocrisy, Pretense
s.d: to give an impression of having certain purposes or motivations, while in reality having quite different ones
s.g: to pretend; to act hypocritically; pretense; hypocrisy
s.c: In a number of languages ὑποκρίνομαι and ὑπόκρισις are expressed in idiomatic ways, for example, ‘to have two faces,’ ‘to have two tongues,’ ‘to be two people,’ or ‘to have two hearts.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Hypocrisy, Pretense
s.d: to give an impression of having certain purposes or motivations, while in reality having quite different ones
s.g: to pretend; to act hypocritically; pretense; hypocrisy
s.c: In a number of languages ὑποκρίνομαι and ὑπόκρισις are expressed in idiomatic ways, for example, ‘to have two faces,’ ‘to have two tongues,’ ‘to be two people,’ or ‘to have two hearts.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Hypocrisy, Pretense
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὑποκρίνομαι<SDBG:ὑποκρίνομαι:000000>} ‘to pretend,’ {D:88.227}) one who pretends to be other than he really is
s.g: hypocrite; pretender; one who acts hypocritically

s.d: to cause to ascend
s.g: to make ascend; to take up

s.d: to respond to what has been said (in the NT restricted to responses to questions)
s.g: to reply to respond

s.d: to assist in supplying what may be needed{N:001}
s.g: to help

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Suppose, Think Possible
s.d: to regard something as presumably true, but without particular certainty
s.g: to suppose; to presume; to assume; to imagine; to believe; to think
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ‘to suppose’ or ‘to presume’ is ‘to think somewhat’ or ‘to think perhaps’ or ‘to think a little.’ In some instances the lack of certainty is spelled out clearly as ‘to think, but not with certainty’ or ‘to think, but not to know’ or ‘to think, but not to be sure.’

s.dp: Existence in Space › Leave in a Place
s.d: to be left behind, with the implication of continuing to exist
s.g: to be left behind; to be left; to remain

s.d: a trough placed beneath the wine press to receive the grape juice pressed out
s.g: wine trough

s.d: to cause to continue to exist subsequent to some temporal reference point
s.g: to cause to remain after; to leave behind

s.d: to resist by holding one’s ground
s.g: to resist; to hold one’s ground; to not be moved
s.c: For another interpretation of ὑπομένω in ⟦James 1:12|James 1:12⟧, see LN 68.17.

s.d: to stay longer in a place than one is expected to
s.g: to stay behind; to remain longer than

s.d: to continue in an activity or state despite resistance and opposition
s.g: to continue; to remain; to endure
s.c: For another interpretation of ὑπομένω in ⟦James 1:12|James 1:12⟧, see LN 39.20.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Patience, Endurance, Perseverance
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὑπομονή<SDBG:ὑπομονή:000000>} ‘endurance,’ {D:25.174}) to continue to bear up despite difficulty and suffering
s.g: to endure; to bear up; to demonstrate endurance; to put up with

s.dp: Memory and Recall › Recalling from Memory
s.d: to cause to recall and to think about again
s.g: to remind; to cause to remember; to cause to think about again

s.dp: Memory and Recall › Recalling from Memory
s.d: to cause oneself to remember or to be caused to remember
s.g: to recall; to remember

s.dp: Memory and Recall › Recalling from Memory
s.d: to cause to recall and to think about again
s.g: to remind; to cause to remember; to cause to think about again
s.c: In ⟦2 Timothy 1:5|2 Timothy 1:5⟧ the phrase ὑπόμνησιν λαμβάνω may be interpreted as a causative passive phrase (compare λαμβάνω in LN 90.63 and LN 90.85), for example, ὑπόμνησιν λαβὼν τῆς ἐν σοὶ ἀνυποκρίτου πίστεως ‘I have been reminded of your sincere faith,’ but it may also be appropriately rendered as an instance of active remembering and accordingly translated as ‘I remember the sincere faith that you have.’|It is also possible to interpret ὑπόμνησις in ⟦2 Peter 1:13|2 Peter 1:13⟧ as meaning simply ‘to remember,’ and therefore one may translate as ‘to stir you up as you remember.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Patience, Endurance, Perseverance
s.d: capacity to continue to bear up under difficult circumstances
s.g: endurance; being able to endure

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Suppose, Think Possible
s.d: to have an opinion based on scant evidence, often with the implication of regarding a false opinion as true
s.g: to imagine; to conjecture; to suspect; to falsely suspect; to be suspicious; suspicion

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Suppose, Think Possible
s.d: to have an opinion based on scant evidence, often with the implication of regarding a false opinion as true
s.g: to imagine; to conjecture; to suspect; to falsely suspect; to be suspicious; suspicion

s.d: to sail or move along beside some object which provides a degree of protection or shelter
s.g: to sail under the shelter of; to sail on; protected by

s.d: a gentle blowing of the wind
s.g: to blow gently
s.c: In some instances a gentle wind may be described as ‘the air was just moving’ or ‘the air could just barely be felt’ or ‘the wind was just touching the skin.’

s.d: a piece of furniture on which one may rest one’s feet
s.g: footstool
s.c: Since footstools are a common cultural feature in many parts of the world, it is rarely necessary to use a descriptive phrase. One can, however, use an expression such as ‘a thing on which to rest one’s feet.’ In some languages the functional equivalent of a footstool is a ‘footstick,’ that is to say, a stick on which one normally places the feet in order to raise them from the relatively damp dirt floor of a typical house or hut.

s.d: (an idiom, literally: footstool of the feet) to be under the complete control of someone
s.g: under the complete control of
s.c: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to preserve the idiom ‘under the feet of,’ though in some instances one may use a parallel idiom, for example, ‘to stand on,’ so that ⟦1 Corinthians 15:25|1 Corinthians 15:25⟧ might be rendered ‘until he stands on all his enemies,’ but it is more likely that the idiom in this context is better rendered as ‘until he defeats all his enemies.’

s.d: the essential or basic nature of an entity
s.g: substance; nature; essence; real being
s.c: In some languages there is no ready lexical equivalent of ‘real being’ or ‘nature.’ Therefore, one may express this concept in ⟦Hebrews 1:3|Hebrews 1:3⟧ as ‘who is … just like what he really is.’

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Trust, Rely
s.d: that which provides the basis for trust and reliance
s.g: trust; confidence; assurance

s.d: to hold oneself back from doing something, with the implication of some fearful concern
s.g: to hold back from; to shrink from; to avoid
s.c: For another interpretation of ὑποστέλλω in ⟦Acts 20:27|Acts 20:27⟧, see LN 68.53.

s.d: to cease doing something of presumed positive value because of adverse circumstances or fear
s.g: to cease; to stop; to give up doing
s.c: It is also possible to translate this clause in ⟦Galatians 2:12|Galatians 2:12⟧ as ‘he withdrew and separated himself.’ For another interpretation of ὑποστέλλω in ⟦Acts 20:27|Acts 20:27⟧, see LN 13.160.

s.d: to cease doing something of presumed positive value because of adverse circumstances or fear
s.g: to cease; to stop; to give up doing
s.c: In ⟦Hebrews 10:39|Hebrews 10:39⟧ ὑποστολῆς serves as an aspect of an implied πίστις, which occurs in ⟦Hebrews 10:38|Hebrews 10:38⟧.

s.d: to move back to a point from which one has previously departed
s.g: to return; to go back; to come back

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Change an Opinion Concerning Truth
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ὑποστρέφω<SDBG:ὑποστρέφω:000000>}[a] ‘to return,’ {D:15.88}) to turn back to a previous belief
s.g: to turn back again to; to change to a former belief; to turn back from

s.d: to be again in a former state
s.g: to return to again; to again be in

s.d: to spread out something underneath
s.g: to spread out; to spread out under

s.d: submission to the orders or directives of someone
s.g: obedience; submission

s.d: to bring something under the firm control of someone
s.g: to subject to; to bring under control

s.d: to submit to the orders or directives of someone
s.g: to obey; to submit to; obedience; submission

s.d: to provide instruction as to what should be done
s.g: to instruct; to give instructions

s.dp: Danger, Risk, Safe, Save › Expose Oneself to Danger
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to put down the neck) willingly and purposely to expose oneself to extreme danger and risk
s.g: to risk one’s life
s.c: In some instances one can translate this expression in ⟦Romans 16:4|Romans 16:4⟧ as ‘who showed they were willing to die in order that I could live’ or ‘in order to help me continue to live, they almost died.’

s.d: to sail or move along beside some object which provides a degree of protection or shelter
s.g: to sail under the shelter of; to sail on; protected by

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Pattern, Model, Example, and Corresponding Representation
s.d: a model of behavior as an example to be imitated or to be avoided
s.g: model; example

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Patience, Endurance, Perseverance
s.d: to continue to bear up despite difficulty and suffering
s.g: to endure; to bear up; to demonstrate endurance; to put up with

s.dp: Linear Movement › Leave, Depart, Flee, Escape, Send
s.d: to move away from a location, implying a considerable distance
s.g: to withdraw; to retire; to go off; to go away

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Worry, Anxiety, Distress, Peace
s.d: to cause great annoyance to and thus to wear someone out
s.g: to annoy and wear out; to wear someone down by annoying

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Self-Control, Lack of Self-Control
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὑπωπιάζω ‘to strike the eye,’ not occurring in the NT) to keep one’s body under complete control, with the implication of rough treatment given to the body, possibly as an aspect of discipline (a meaning evidently taken from the language of prize-fighting)
s.g: to keep under control; to exercise self-control
